To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

d-amphetamine causes neural degeneration in frontal cortex and neostriatum, that damage to neostriatum is likely to include damage to dopamine terminals, that damage in frontal motor areas is likely to include both axonal damage and cell body damage to non-monomamine neurons and that the degree of damage in frontal motor cortex is constrained by genetic factors.
chronic amphetamine administration induces degeneration in neocortex and striatum of rats.
d-amphetamine causes degenerative changes in neostriatal and cortical neurons of rats.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of amphetamine on the brain, and in particular, the effects of chronic amphetamine exposure on the brain.
the mechanisms of amphetamine-induced degeneration.
the neurotoxic effects of d-amphetamine.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
amphetamine-induced degeneration in neocortex and neostriatum is due to a direct effect of amphetamine on neurons and not to a consequence of the drug-induced behavioral activation and hyperthermia.
amphetamine induces degeneration in neosriatal dopamine axons and in non-monoamine cortical neurons.

amphetamine-induced degeneration of non-monoamine cells in frontal cortex and neostriatum is a dose-dependent process, which is more severe in the frontal cortex of the Long-Evans strain of rat than in Sprague-Daweley rats, and which is not associated with a loss of monoamine neurons or fibers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
amphetamine induces damage to dopamine axons in neostriatal areas and to non-monoaminergic neurons in frontal motor areas and somatosensory cortex.
d-amphetamine causes degenerative changes in neostriatal dopamine axons and terminals and in non-dopamine cortical areas.
amphetamine-induced damage is not limited to the dopamine terminals in the striatum, but includes non-dopamine cells, possibly in frontal motor cortex, that are involved in motor control.
The main takeaway from our work is that
chronic amphetamine treatment causes damage in both the neostriatal and cortical dopamine systems, but that the pattern of damage is different in the two systems.
amphetamine can damage brain regions other than those that are directly affected by the drug.
amphetamine causes degeneration of non-monoamine axons, including those in the frontal motor cortex and the neostriatal dopamine terminal field.
